processing: Not a processed leaf but a dish: tea leaves are fried in tea-seed oil with ginger, garlic and often peanuts, pounded in the pan with a hooked mallet, then boiled with water and strained.
harvest_season: Made all year from stored leaf. In the Yao tradition of Gongcheng, leaf picked around Grain Rain in spring is thought best, then dried and kept above the hearth.
appearance_dry: Before cooking, plain dried tea leaf, often darkened by storage over the hearth.
appearance_liquor: Cloudy and golden-brown, with a sheen of oil, served over toppings in a bowl.
appearance_wet: The pounded leaf is broken and dark, and is strained away before serving.
taste_profile: Savoury and pungent: strong tea bitterness softened by oil, with hot ginger and garlic, and the crunch of puffed rice and peanuts.

brewing.notes: Amounts are a rough home guide, since every household differs. Fry the leaf with ginger and garlic in hot tea-seed oil, pound until golden and fragrant, add water, boil, strain into bowls over puffed rice and peanuts.

vintage_note: Not sold by year or season. It is cooked at home from whatever dried leaf the household keeps, and the only commercial versions are ready mixes and instant packets. Fresh leaf and fresh oil matter far more than any vintage.
description:
Da You Cha means roughly 'beaten oil tea', and it is closer to a soup than to a steeped tea. It belongs to the Yao people of the Nanling mountains, with main centres at Gongcheng in Guangxi and in Hunan counties including Jiangyong, Chengbu and Daoxian. Neighbouring Zhuang and Han communities took it up too, and the Dong of Sanjiang in Guangxi have it among their everyday customs.

The pounding is the heart of it. Leaf goes into a hot iron pan with tea-seed oil, ginger, garlic and often peanuts, and gets beaten with a hooked mallet until it turns golden and smells toasted. Then water goes in, it all boils, and the broth is strained off the leaf.

It arrives in a bowl over puffed rice, peanuts, rice cakes or herbs such as scallion and coriander. Expect bitterness up front, then heat from the ginger and a rich, oily body. People who dislike the first bowl often come round by the second, and custom usually means you will be offered at least three.

There is no grade to shop for. If you want to try it at home, use a sturdy dried green or dark leaf and real tea-seed oil, and do not rush the pounding. Recipes differ from village to village, so no single version is the correct one.
history:
A local account in Gongcheng dates the habit to the Tang dynasty, over a thousand years back; that is tradition, not a documented date. What is firmly dated is its recognition: China placed the Yao oil-tea custom, declared by Gongcheng, on the national intangible heritage list in 2021, and it was inscribed by UNESCO in 2022 as part of China's traditional tea practices. Chengbu oil tea joined Hunan's provincial list in 2009.

It has been passed on mainly through families and village elders. Today it also appears as a festival and tourist dish, in Gongcheng and in Sanjiang.
